text: Countdown is a British game show featuring word and mathematical tasks that began airing on 2 November 1982 and is broadcast on Channel 4. It was the first programme to be broadcast on Channel 4 and has aired 92 series since its debut, with over 8,000 episodes, making it one of Britain's longest-running game shows. The original French version, Des chiffres et des lettres (Numbers & Letters), ran on French television from 1965 until 2024. Each episode features two contestants competing in three game types: a ten-letter round where they attempt to form the longest word from nine randomly selected letters, a four numbers round in which they use arithmetic to reach a random target from six numbers, and a conundrum, a buzzer round to solve a nine-letter anagram. During series heats, the winning contestant returns the next day until they either lose or retire with eight wins as an undefeated "Octochamp"; the best eight contestants are invited to the series finals, decided in knockout format. Contestants of exceptional skill have received national media coverage, and the show is widely recognised and parodied in British culture. Produced by Yorkshire Television, Countdown was recorded at The Leeds Studios for 27 years before moving to Granada Studios in 2009 and then to Dock10 in Greater Manchester in 2013 following the development of MediaCityUK. Richard Whiteley presented the show for 23 years until his death on 26 June 2005; after his death, Des Lynam presented from October 2005 to December 2006, Des O'Connor from January 2007 to December 2008, Jeff Stelling from January 2009 to December 2011, and Nick Hewer from January 2012 until his retirement in June 2021, with Colin Murray standing in for him during part of the COVID-19 pandemic. Anne Robinson presented from June 2021 to July 2022, after which Murray returned on 14 July as a stand-in host. On 25 July 2022, Les Dennis guest hosted from 4 to 15 August, followed by Jenny Eclair from 16 to 19 August after Murray tested positive for COVID-19. Guest hosts including Floella Benjamin, Richard Coles, Trevor McDonald (for a second time), and Moira Stuart hosted one week each during the show's 40th anniversary celebrations in 2022. Murray was named the permanent host in January 2023. In the early years, the show had multiple assistant presenters: Carol Vorderman, hired for Series 1 as "vital statistician," alternated with Dr Linda Barrett until Barrett left after Series 2; letters were initially placed by Cathy Hytner, then by Karen Loughlin in Series 14 (1987) and Lucy Summers in Series 17 (early 1989); numbers were handled by Beverley Isherwood, later taken over by Hytner mid-Series 3. From Series 18 (July 1989) onwards, Vorderman permanently handled both letters and numbers. After 26 years, she left in December 2008 (alongside O'Connor) and was replaced by Rachel Riley, who has held the role since January 2009. Dr Anne-Marie Imafidon stood in for Riley from December 2021 to March 2022, and Dr Tom Crawford, an Oxford and Cambridge lecturer, stood in for Riley for three weeks in early 2025, making his first appearance on 24 February as the show's first-ever male arithmetician. Susie Dent first appeared in June 1992 as a rotating lexicographer and became a recurring member in 2003; since 2005 she has been the sole lexicographer and has been credited as a co-presenter since January 2015, appearing in "Dictionary Corner" with a weekly celebrity guest. Notable past lexicographers who appeared in more than 100 episodes include Catherine Clarke, Damian Eadie, Alison Heard, Mark Nyman, Richard Samson, Julia Swannell, Della Thompson, Freda Thornton, and Yvonne Warburton. The show originated from the French format Des chiffres et des lettres, created by Armand Jammot, which debuted in September 1965 under the name Le Mot Le Plus Long (The Longest Word) before adding numbers in January 1972. Belgian record executive Marcel Stellman brought the format to Britain, proposing it to several networks. Yorkshire Television purchased the concept in 1981 and produced two non-televised pilot episodes under the title Calendar Countdown, aired in Yorkshire between April and June 1982. Richard Whiteley, who hosted the spin-off, earned the nickname "Twice Nightly Whiteley" due to his daily appearances on both Calendar and the spin-off. He was assisted by Cathy Hytner and Denise McFarland-Cruickshanks for letters and numbers, Robina Sharp for selecting numbers and operating a fruit machine for the target, and Angela Garbut as the vital statistician; Ted Moult, who appeared in the pilot episodes and throughout the regional series, was the first Dictionary Corner guest and only appeared in the first seven episodes. After an additional, unbroadcast pilot episode with a refined format, the show was bought by Channel 4, which launched in November 1982. The show was renamed Countdown, expanded its hosting team, and was initially commissioned for four times a week for seven weeks, but due to its success, it has continued to be recommissioned as of 2024. A proposed spin-off, Junior Countdown, hosted by Gyles Brandreth and Ted Moult, was abandoned after a flawed pilot. Countdown was the first programme broadcast by Channel 4 on 2 November 1982, with Whiteley opening with the line: "As the countdown to a brand new channel ends, a brand new Countdown begins." Production staff recruited additional hostesses through national newspaper ads, with clear emphasis on mathematical skill for number experts; Beverley Isherwood and Linda Barrett were hired to handle number and letter tile selection, and a lexicographer was required for Dictionary Corner to verify words and provide entertainment. The lexicographer role was traditionally filled by an Oxford University Press member or production staff member, with past guests including Nigel Rees, Jo Brand, Martin Jarvis, Richard Digance, Geoffrey Durham, Ken Bruce, Magnus Magnusson, Pam Ayres, Paul Zenon, Jenny Eclair, Al Murray, John Sergeant, and Gyles Brandreth. Over time, the additional hostesses were dropped, retaining Vorderman primarily for tile selection and calculation verification. The role of lexicographer rotated among over thirty individuals until January 2005, when Susie Dent was permanently appointed after her 1992 debut. On 26 June 2005, Richard Whiteley died after a failed heart operation; the episode scheduled for that day was postponed as a mark of respect, with no episode aired, and the remaining episodes were broadcast after his death, preceded by a tribute from Carol Vorderman. The show went into hiatus from 1 July to determine its next steps, with no repeats aired. In October 2005, Des Lynam took over as main presenter, having previously participated in Celebrity Countdown in April 1998; his tenure ended in December 2006 due to a demanding schedule, with viewers reacting angrily to a proposed move from Leeds to Worthing. In January 2007, Des O'Connor took over; during his tenure, Susie Dent went on maternity leave in 2007–2008, with Alison Heard temporarily replacing her until 6 February 2008. By July 2008, both O'Connor and Vorderman announced they would leave at the end of that year after Series 59; O'Connor left to focus on other projects, and Vorderman left after rejecting a 33% salary decrease and being offered a 90% cut, with her agent stating the show could survive without her. Media reports suggested Rory Bremner or Alexander Armstrong as possible successors, but both declined. Several prominent women, including Anthea Turner, Ulrika Jonsson, and Myleene Klass, were considered, but Channel 4 selected an unknown male or female arithmetician with "charm and charisma." When Lynam became presenter, the show drew an average of 1.7 million viewers daily, around half a million more than in Whiteley's final years; the Series 54 final on 26 May 2006 attracted 2.5 million viewers. Daily viewership had previously ranged from 3 to 4 million in its 16:15 slot, and a drop in viewership after scheduling changes led Labour MP Jonathan Shaw to propose returning the show to a later time. The show has since moved to 14:10 as of 2025. In November 2008, Jeff Stelling was confirmed as host, and Rachel Riley was confirmed as Vorderman's replacement. Stelling left in December 2011 due to football commitments with Sky Sports, and Nick Hewer was announced as his replacement, taking over on 9 January 2012. During the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic, Colin Murray filled in for Hewer during his isolation. Des O'Connor died on 14 November 2020 after a fall at home; the episode aired two days later was dedicated to his memory. On 7 December 2020, Hewer announced he would step down at the end of Series 83 in summer 2021, calling it a "privilege and a pleasure." On 15 February 2021, Anne Robinson, who first appeared in Dictionary Corner in 1987, was announced as Hewer's successor, beginning Series 84. Hewer's final episode aired on 25 June 2021. On 28 June 2021, Robinson became the show's first female host in its 39-year history. In May 2022, it was announced she would leave after one year, with Murray taking over for most of Series 86; she recorded 265 episodes, equivalent to two full series and the first three weeks of Series 86. The show quickly gained cult status in British television and maintains that image today, with its audience primarily consisting of students, homemakers, and pensioners due to its "teatime" broadcast slot and inclusive format. It has been one of Channel 4's most-watched programmes for over twenty years but has never won a major television award. Each episode awards the winner of the reigning champion (or the championship when two new contestants compete) a teapot styled to resemble the clock used in each round, introduced in December 1998 and custom-made, obtainable only by winning. Defeated contestants and retiring undefeated champions receive Countdown-themed merchandise. Initially, the series winner received a leather-bound copy of the twenty-volume Oxford English Dictionary, worth over £4,000; David Acton (Series 31 winner) opted for a CD-ROM version due to veganism and donated the price difference to charity. Between 2011 and 2021, the prize included ordinary hardback twenty-one-volume dictionaries, a laptop, and a lifetime subscription to Oxford Online (replaced by a MacBook Pro from Series 68); the physical dictionaries were discontinued after Series 83 as obsolete. Since Series 54 in 2006, the series champion also receives the Richard Whiteley Memorial Trophy. Runner-up prizes in finals increased from a £100 book voucher to £250, then £500, then £1,000, and from Series 68, the runner-up wins a laptop. The first episode was repeated on 1 October 2007 on More4 and on 2 November 2007 on Channel 4 as part of Channel 4 at 25, a 25th-anniversary celebration. On 2 November 2007, the show celebrated its 25th anniversary with a special 'birthday episode' featuring 2006 winner Conor Travers and 2002 winner Chris Wills; VIP guests selected the letters and numbers. Guests included Gordon Brown, Amir Khan, and Richard Attenborough. A statement from France Télévisions was read by Carol Vorderman to commend Channel 4 on the success of Countdown.

The series champion of Countdown receives the Richard Whiteley Memorial Trophy in memory of the show's original presenter. Runner-up prizes in the finals have increased over the years from a £100 book voucher to £250, then to £500, and finally to £1,000, with beginning in Series 68, the runner-up wins a laptop. The first episode of Countdown was repeated on 1 October 2007 on More4 and on 2 November 2007 on Channel 4 as part of Channel 4 at 25, a celebration of its 25th birthday. On 2 November 2007, Countdown aired a special 'birthday episode' to mark its 25th anniversary, featuring 2006 winner Conor Travers and 2002 winner Chris Wills as players, with VIP guests selecting the letters and numbers; guests included Gordon Brown, Amir Khan, and Richard Attenborough. A statement from the French TV network France Télévisions was read by Carol Vorderman to commend Channel 4 on Countdown's success. On 26 March 2010, Queen Elizabeth II congratulated Countdown for reaching 5,000 episodes, and on 5 September 2014, the programme received a Guinness World Record at the end of its 6,000th show for being the longest-running television programme of its kind during Series 71. Countdown has occupied a daytime broadcast slot since its inception in a 30-minute format, and since 2001, episodes last around 45 minutes including advertising breaks. During normal series, the winner of each game returns for the next day's show; a player who wins eight games is declared an "octochamp" and retires. At the end of each series, the eight best players—ranked first by number of wins and then by total score to break ties—are invited back for the series finals, where they compete in a knockout tournament seeded so that the first plays the eighth, the second plays the seventh, and so on. The winner of the knockout, culminating in the Grand Final, becomes the series champion. Each series lasts approximately six months with about 125 episodes. Approximately every four series, a Champion of Champions tournament occurs, inviting sixteen of the best players since the previous championship, selected by producer Damian Eadie, typically including series winners and other notable contestants. Series 33 was designated a "Supreme Championship," in which 56 of the best contestants from all prior series participated in a knockout tournament, with Series 10 champion Harvey Freeman declared Supreme Champion after defeating Allan Saldanha in the final. There are also occasional special episodes featuring past contestants in themed matches, such as David Acton and Kenneth Michie returning for a rematch of their Series 31 final, and brothers Sanjay and Sandeep Mazumder playing against each other on 20 December 2004. Since the shift to 45-minute episodes, the game is divided into three sections with advertising breaks. The first section includes two letters rounds and one numbers round; the second includes two letters rounds and one numbers round, followed by the Dictionary Corner anecdote, then two further letters rounds and one numbers round; the third section includes two letters rounds, Susie Dent's "Origins of Words" feature since September 2007, two further letters rounds, one numbers round, and a final "Conundrum" puzzle. Contestants swap control after every round, so each has five letters rounds and two numbers rounds. Since Series 46 in 2001, the host poses a "Teatime Teaser" at the end of the first two sections, giving a set of short words and a cryptic clue to a single word that can be anagrammed from them, with the solution revealed at the start of the next section; the anagram length has varied between seven and nine letters. The contestant in control chooses between two stacks of face-down letter tiles—one with vowels (A-E-I-O-U) and one with consonants—and the assistant reveals the top tile, repeating this nine times to form a nine-letter group with at least three vowels and four consonants. Contestants have 30 seconds to form the longest valid single word using the letters, with no letter used more than it appears; letter frequencies are weighted according to natural English usage, similar to Scrabble, and are periodically altered by producers. The two stacks are not replenished between rounds. Both contestants write down their words; after time runs out, the host asks for declared word lengths, starting with the contestant who chose the letters. If one has not written their word, they must state this; if both declare the same length, the one who chose the letters must give their word first to prevent cheating. If both state they have not written their words, the host allows a moment to do so, typically edited out. The contestant with the longer valid word scores one point per letter or 18 points if all nine are used. If the words are identical or of the same length, both score. If a contestant is visually impaired, Dictionary Corner verifies the word. Inaccurate declarations of word length result in zero points, even if the word is valid. Dictionary Corner reveals the longest and any unusual words formed from the letters at the end of each round. Most words in the Oxford Dictionary of English are valid, as are accepted forms not explicitly listed. Words not allowed include those that are not in the dictionary or not in accepted forms. The contestant in control selects six of 24 shuffled number tiles—two each of numbers 1 to 10 (small numbers) and four large numbers (25, 50, 75, 100)—and decides how many large numbers to use, after which the tiles are randomly drawn and placed on the board. A random three-digit target from 100 to 999 is generated by "CECIL" (Countdown's Electronic Calculator In Leeds). Contestants have 30 seconds to find a sequence of calculations using the numbers and basic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division), not using any number more than it appears, and only exact division is allowed; fractions and negative numbers are not permitted. Both contestants must declare their results, and if both declare the same result and have not written their calculations down, the one who made the selection goes first. The contestant whose result is closer to the target scores points: ten for exact match, seven for within one to five, five for within six to ten; no points if more than ten away, or if calculations are flawed, too slow, or not written down. Both score if they reach the same result or are equally close. If neither reaches the target exactly, the assistant attempts a solution. Some games have multiple exact solutions; for example, 7 × (75 + 50 + 2 – 8 – 3) = 812. Not all games are solvable, especially when six small numbers are chosen and the target is large. Selecting one large and five small numbers is the most common choice, though two large numbers offer the best chance of an exact solution; selections with zero or four large numbers are generally considered hardest. The 24 tiles are laid out in four rows, with the top row containing only the large numbers; the contestant may specify how many tiles to draw from each row or simply state how many large and small numbers to use, with the assistant drawing them randomly. Numbers are usually placed from right to left, starting with small ones, though sometimes in scrambled order. On rare occasions, the contestant makes no choice, and the assistant selects the tiles. Unlike the letters round, the number tiles are fully replenished after each numbers round. A special edition on 15 March 2010 for previous champions Kirk Bevins and Chris Davies used instead of the four large numbers, the numbers 12, 37, and two unrevealed numbers. In a further special broadcast on 16 August 2010 between Series 59 finalists Charlie Reams and Junaid Mubeen, the other two numbers were revealed as 62 and 87. The final round is the Countdown Conundrum, where contestants are shown a combination of two or three words totaling nine letters and must form a single word using all letters in 30 seconds, buzzing in to respond (a bell for the champion, a buzzer for the challenger). Each contestant is allowed only one guess; the first to answer correctly scores 10 points. If a contestant buzzes in and either responds incorrectly or fails to respond, they are frozen out and the remaining time is given to the opponent. If neither solves it, the presenter asks the audience if anyone knows the answer and chooses someone to call it out (this practice was temporarily stopped in 2009 due to camera angle issues after a studio change). The Conundrum is intended to have one solution, though on occasion more than one valid word is found (e.g., MISSATTEE can become ESTIMATES or STEAMIEST), and any such result is accepted. On rare occasions, the Conundrum is presented as a nine-letter word to be anagrammed into another (e.g., SMARTENED becoming TRADESMEN). If the contestants' scores are within ten points going into the Conundrum, it is called a "Crucial Countdown Conundrum"; since ten points are at stake, solving it will either win the game or force a tiebreaker. If scores are tied after the Conundrum, additional Conundrums are played until the tie is broken. There have been several instances with two Conundrums to decide the winner, but only a handful of episodes required three, and there have been rare cases requiring even more, though not all such episodes are included in the broadcast. The rules of Countdown are derived from Des chiffres et des lettres, with the main difference being round length—DCedL's number rounds are 45 seconds, Countdown's are 30 seconds. DCedL also features "duels" with short tasks like mental arithmetic, forming themed words, or spelling correctly. Other differences include a different scoring system (9 points for exact solution, 6 for closest in DCedL) and a different proportion of letters to numbers rounds (10 to 4 in Countdown, 8 to 4 in DCedL). The pilot episode had different rules: only eight letters were selected per letters round; if two contestants offered a word of the same length or equally close solution in a numbers game, only the contestant who selected the round received points; five points were awarded for an exact numbers solution, three for within five, and one point for the closer solution regardless of distance. The style and colour scheme of the set have changed many times, and the show moved to Manchester after over 25 years in Leeds, but the clock has always been the centrepiece, and the clock music composed by Alan Hawkshaw remains a well-recognized feature. Executive producer John Meade commissioned Hawkshaw to revise the music for extra intensity at the start of Series 31 in January 1996, but after hundreds of viewer complaints, the original tune was reinstated after just 12 shows. The original set, known as the Pastel set, was used from 1982 until Series 17 in early 1989. A brown wooden set was introduced in Series 18 in July 1989 but remained in use for less than two years. Series 22 in July 1991 introduced the familiar "Wings" set in red, used until 1995. Series 31 in January 1996 changed the colour scheme to purple, then to tangerine at the end of 1999 with updated score and CECIL displays. In January 2003, the set was updated to a pink and purple striped theme with the letters and numbers boards on separate islands. In January 2009, a new numerical blue theme was introduced with the boards on opposite sides of a single display stand. New modern displays for scores and numbers came in January 2013, and a slight redesign occurred in July 2017 while retaining the blue background used up to the most recent series. The original clock was used until September 2013, when it was replaced. Until the end of Series 21, if contestants had equal scores after the first conundrum, the match was declared a draw and both returned for the next show. A significant format change occurred in September 2001, when the show expanded from nine rounds and 30 minutes to the current fifteen rounds and 45 minutes. The older format was split into two halves, each with three letters and one numbers game, plus a conundrum at the end of the second half. Under the old format, Grand Finals were extended to fourteen rounds, but now all shows use the fifteen-round format. The rules regarding valid words have changed over time; American spelling was allowed until 2002, and more unspecified inflections were assumed valid. In September 2007, Susie Dent began the "Origin of Words" feature, which follows the eighth letters round, partway through the third section of each episode; it was omitted during her maternity leave and reinstated upon her return. When the 15-round format was first introduced in September 2001, the round composition differed from today's: each of the first two sections had four letters rounds and one numbers round, and the third section had three letters rounds, one numbers round, and the conundrum. This created an imbalance, with one contestant making letters rounds six times and choosing numbers only once, while the other made letters five times and numbers twice. Dictionary Corner's guest spot was immediately before the first advertising break, and Susie Dent's Origin of Words spot preceded the second numbers game before the second break. The change to the current format was implemented on 25 March 2013, three weeks into the second section of Series 68, to comply with Channel 4's decision to increase advertising and alter its timing, reducing the actual show length from 36 to 35 minutes. Since its debut in 1982, Countdown has had more than 8,600 televised episodes and 92 complete series, and there have been sixteen Champion of Champions tournaments, the most recent in January 2023. Several of the programme's most successful contestants have received national media coverage; teenager Julian Fell set a record score of 146 in December 2002. In 2006, 14-year-old Conor Travers became the youngest series champion in the show's history, and 11-year-old Kai Laddiman became the youngest octochamp in 20 years. Conor Travers went on to win the 30th Anniversary edition.

The first advertising break and Susie Dent's Origin of Words spot occurred just before the second numbers game, shortly before the second break. The format change to the current structure was implemented on 25 March 2013, three weeks into the second section of Series 68, in response to Channel 4's decision to increase advertising and adjust its timing, which reduced Countdown's actual show length from 36 to 35 minutes. Since its debut in 1982, the programme has aired more than 8,600 televised episodes and completed 92 series, with sixteen Champion of Champions tournaments held, the most recent in January 2023. Several top contestants have received national media attention; in December 2002, teenager Julian Fell set a record score of 146. In 2006, 14-year-old Conor Travers became the youngest series champion in the show's history, and 11-year-old Kai Laddiman became the youngest octochamp in 20 years. Conor Travers later won the 30th Anniversary Champion of Champions series in March 2013 with a record-equalling 146. On 17 January 2019, Zarte Siempre, who won that tournament, set a new record of 150, which was surpassed in May 2019 by Elliott Mellor’s 152. On 29 September 2022, Tom Stevenson scored 154, a record later equalled by Cillian McMulkin on 31 January 2023. At eight years old, Tanmay Dixit was the youngest player ever to appear, winning twice in March 2005, and gained press attention for using words like 'fannies' and 'farted' in letters rounds. On Christmas Day 1987, Nic Brown achieved the highest score difference in a standard 14-round game, beating Joel Salkin 108–36, a margin of 72 points, and became one of only two contestants to achieve an undefeated 'grand slam'—becoming an Octochamp, winning a series, and winning a Championship of Champions. In April 2013, Giles Hutchings, a student at Royal Grammar School, Guildford, set the highest octochamp score at 965 points over eight games and won Series 68. This record was later beaten by Dylan Taylor, who scored 974 in August 2013 but lost the Grand Final. In 2019, Elliott Mellor broke the record by 87 points, becoming the first octochamp to surpass 1,000 points with a total of 1,061 over eight games, though he finished as runner-up. Three former contestants have returned to the show’s production team: Michael Wylie, Mark Nyman (as producer and occasional lexicographer in Dictionary Corner), and Damian Eadie (current series producer). In 1998, sixteen celebrities participated in Celebrity Countdown, a series of eight games broadcast weekly over eight weeks, including Des Lynam, who beat Siân Lloyd. In one game, Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall scored 47 against Jilly Goolden, who scored 9, making the highest and lowest scores in the same game. On Christmas Day 1997, Richard Whiteley and Carol Vorderman competed in a special episode, with William G. Stewart hosting in Whiteley’s chair and Susie Dent taking over Vorderman’s role, while Mark Nyman and Magnus Magnusson were in Dictionary Corner. The game was decided by the conundrum 'mistletoe', which Vorderman solved in two seconds after Whiteley accidentally buzzed after one second due to his habit of revealing the conundrum before solving it. Notable contestants include Pete Cashmore (Nuts magazine editor), Ayoola Erinle (rugby player), Neil MacKenzie, Clarke Carlisle, and Matt Le Tissier (footballers), Jon Marsh and Nick Saloman (musicians), Alex Horne (comedian), Peter Sheridan (Irish playwright), and Kirk Bevins (darts referee), who won Series 60 and reached the quarter-finals of the 30th Birthday Championship. Countdown is frequently referenced and parodied in British culture. In 1992, Saint Etienne used the host’s lead-in as the opening for "Stoned to Say the Least". In the 2002 film About a Boy, protagonist Will Freeman is a regular viewer. The Doctor Who episodes "Bad Wolf" (2005) and "Last of the Time Lords" (2007) reference a futuristic version of Countdown, with Professor Docherty commenting on the show’s change after Des Lynam took over. Fairport Convention guitarist Simon Nicol titled one of his albums Consonant Please Carol, echoing a show catchphrase. The show is mentioned in episode one of series 4 of Misfits (2012). A Countdown video game was released for the Nintendo DS and Wii in 2009, and mobile apps have also been developed. The programme has generated numerous widely viewed outtakes, including a round where the word 'gobshite' was offered, featured in TV's Finest Failures (aired 10 January 2000), and a 1991 episode where contestants Gino Corr and Lawrence Pearse both declared 'wankers', which was edited out but later appeared on outtakes. On 21 October 2008, Charlie Reams declared 'wankers', which was kept in but the word was bleeped. Other instances with mildly offensive words, such as 'wanker' or 'fart' (as the first four letters on the board in a 2001 episode, also featured in 100 Greatest TV Moments from Hell), and an anagram of 'fucked' appearing as 'A U O D F C K E G' (without either player using the word or Dictionary Corner finding two seven-letter words) have been aired. On 2 February 2017, the letters round board was 'M T H I A E D H S', and Dictionary Corner found 'shithead', which was bleeped in audio and censored on screen with a poo emoji. The show is referenced in episodes of Father Ted ("The Old Grey Whistle Theft"), Still Game ("Wireless"), Little Britain (2003), and BBC sketch show Dead Ringers, which parodies it multiple times. The Big Breakfast also parodied it in a feature called "Countdown Under". In a sketch "Countdown to Hell" from A Bit of Fry and Laurie, Stephen Fry mocked Richard Whiteley’s punning style and Hugh Laurie played a contestant, while Gyles Brandreth (played by Steve Steen) presented with the letters 'bollocsk' and produced the non-word 'sloblock' (meant to be equivalent to 'bollocks'). The show is briefly referenced in The Office when Chris 'Finchy' Finch mocks a temporary worker by saying he was 'professor in charge of watching Countdown every day', commenting on its student audience and the fact that viewers during its 'hometime' slot cannot be at work. The format has been parodied on Have I Got News for You: in 1999, during Whiteley’s guest appearance, the numbers game and clock music were copied, ending with the conundrum 'PHANIOILS' whose answer was Ian Hislop; in 2004, during Vorderman’s guest appearance, a news-based conundrum round was introduced; in 2006, when Vorderman hosted the show, a 'Spinning Conundrum Numbers Round' was introduced, combining a news picture with a number puzzle. In 1998, Richard Whiteley was the victim of a practical joke on Noel's House Party, where contestants and rounds were planted in a 'Gotcha!' prank. Both contestants and Dictionary Corner missed the word in 'OMETHINGS', and both declared 'I've got diarrhoea'. In the numbers round, the male contestant 'answered' by combining 6, 2, and 3 to make 623. Whiteley discovered the joke when Noel Edmonds appeared on set and revealed the short conundrum 'HOGCAT' meant 'gotcha'. In a 2003 episode of Top Gear, Whiteley participated in the 'Star in a Reasonably Priced Car' segment, with Jeremy Clarkson playing a Countdown game with him using words like 'imin' (Mini), 'sexul' (Lexus), 'nevor lard' (Land Rover), 'mushi bits' (Mitsubishi), and 'pianos shiazu' (Hispano-Suiza). The show was referenced twice on Harry Hill's TV Burp: once when 'Dev' (Coronation Street) made a sound like the Countdown end-of-round beep, and again when the competition 'Where Has The Knitted Character Been This Week?' had the answer 'on Rachel Riley's chair'. On 2 July 2010, the game appeared in The IT Crowd’s series 4 episode "The Final Countdown", where Moss declares that the nine-letter string TNETENNBA is a word, later becoming an octochamp and joining an underground club called '8+' to compete in a spoof of Boogie Town, featuring a cameo by Gyles Brandreth. British entertainer Stevie Riks has parodied the show in a YouTube video. In a 2011 episode, the Blackpool-based producer set the conundrum 'PNECRISIS' ('priciness') as a joke about Preston North End’s relegation. The game has also been featured as the first challenge in "What's Next" on Ant and Dec's Saturday Night Takeaway, with the pair versus an old head teacher. In 2010, it was used as a shopping task in the final Channel 4 series of Celebrity Big Brother, where housemates competed against champion Chris Davies via satellite and failed. In 2008, Charlie Reams, who was runner-up in Series 59, created a website called Apterous, allowing online play; all series champions since 2008 have been members. Since 2005, Ben Wilson, champion of Series 46, has organised a Countdown event in Lincoln, known as COLIN, held annually on a Saturday in January. COLIN features three rounds, with players drawn into tables of three (bots used if not divisible by three), each contestant hosting once and playing twice per round. In Round 1, tables are randomly assigned; in Rounds 2 and 3, tables are assigned based on performance. A final is held between the top two players, ranked by wins and points. Since 2014, a hangover event takes place the day after the main event, featuring two rounds with players split into White and Blue teams. In-person events have expanded to other locations, such as Bristol and Edinburgh. Since 2016, most events have been part of 'FOCAL' (Finals of the Co-events Annual League), where players earn points based on performance. The top eight are invited to a final, where they play against each other, and a final is held between the two best players, ranked by wins and points; the winner is declared FOCAL Champion.
